summary: Defines a Management Information Base for monitoring and controlling a Multilink Frame Relay function at the user and network interfaces, following the Frame Relay Forum specification FRF.16. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Several thin pipes can be bundled to act like one big pipe. This gives tools a standard way to watch and control that bundle on an old kind of network.

subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and configuring bundles of physical links that act as one frame relay interface.

tldr.problem: Multilink Frame Relay (FRF.16) lets several physical links act as one frame relay interface, but network managers had no standard SNMP way to configure and monitor those bundles.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module with two scalar objects and three tables, covering bundles, a mapping from interface index to bundle, and bundle links, plus linkUp, linkDown and link-mismatch notifications.
tldr.outcome: Managers get one standard set of objects for MFR devices. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3020 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9141. It defines the MIB for the FRF.16 multilink frame relay function.

sections.title: Multilink Frame Relay Background
sections.content:
RFC 3020 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring and controlling the UNI/NNI Multilink Frame Relay function (MFR). The behaviour being managed was agreed by the Frame Relay Forum in document FRF.16.

MFR provides physical interface emulation for frame relay devices. The emulated interface is made of one or more physical links, called bundle links, aggregated into a single bundle of bandwidth. The RFC notes this is a frame-based inverse multiplexing function, sometimes called an IMUX.

The bundle gives the same order-preserving service as a physical layer for frames sent on a data link connection, and supports all Frame Relay services based on UNI and NNI standards.
sections.eli5: Several small pipes are joined so they look like one big pipe. The water still comes out in the same order it went in.

sections.title: Bundles, Bundle Links and Physical Links
sections.content:
The RFC uses three terms. A physical link is a single physical interface that connects two devices in a frame relay network, for example DS1 or DS0. A bundle is a grouping of one or more physical links using the formats and procedures of multilink frame relay; it works as a logical interface that emulates a single physical interface to the Q.922 data link layer. A bundle link is an MFR sub-component that controls the operation of one of the bundle's physical links.

In the reference model, the bundle sits directly below the Q.922 data link layer, and the bundle links sit between the bundle and the physical layer on each side of the connection.
sections.eli5: The wires are physical links, the rope they make together is the bundle, and each little helper that looks after one wire is a bundle link.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The managed objects consist of two scalar objects and three tables. mfrBundleMaxNumBundles tells the manager the maximum number of bundles the device supports. mfrBundleNextIndex helps a manager choose a value for mfrBundleIndex when creating a row, and can avoid race conditions between several managers creating rows at once (RFC 2494 describes one such algorithm).

The mfrBundleTable is indexed by mfrBundleIndex and configures and monitors bundles. Its columns include the near and far end names, fragmentation settings, hello and acknowledgement timers, a retry count, an activation class and threshold, the sequence number size, the number of links configured and active, the bundle bandwidth and a resequencing error counter.

The bundle-to-ifIndex mapping table is indexed by ifIndex and finds the matching mfrBundleIndex. The mfrBundleLinkTable is also indexed by ifIndex. It holds the state of each bundle link, the far end names, the measured delay, and counters for control frames sent, received and invalid, timer expirations, suspected loopbacks, unexpected sequence numbers and mismatches.

mfrBundleActivationClass controls when a bundle comes up, and mfrBundleSeqNumSize chooses between the standard FRF.12 12-bit sequence number and an optional 24-bit one. Bundle link states follow Annex A of FRF.16.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a set of forms. One form is filled in for each bundle and one for each little helper, and there are two sticky notes with simple facts like how many bundles there can be.

sections.title: Relationship With Other MIBs
sections.content:
Each bundle and each bundle link appears as an interface in the ifTable. Bundle links are indexed in the MFR tables by their ifIndex. Bundles use a separate mfrBundleIndex, which may differ from the bundle's ifIndex. The RFC explains why: the ifTable has no RowStatus, the manager must choose the index of a creatable row, and RFC 2863 suggests the agent should choose ifIndex values. Two indices let the agent implementer manage ifIndex freely.

Several ifTable objects take on specific meaning. For a bundle, ifSpeed is its current bandwidth and ifInErrors and ifOutErrors count frame errors, not fragment errors. For a bundle link, those error counters cover both frame and fragment errors.

In the interface stack table, each bundle link is a lower layer of its bundle, and the bundle is a lower layer of a frame relay service or UNI. A bundle corresponds one-to-one with a DLCMI or UNI in the frame relay DTE MIB tables and with a frame relay service logical port.

The RFC's worked example has two bundles, numbered 10 and 20, each made of two T1 links, carried on four T1 interfaces in all.
sections.eli5: Every bundle and helper also gets a number in the device's big list of connections. The bundle keeps its own second number so that people setting it up and the device itself do not trip over each other.

sections.title: Creating Bundles and Bundle Links
sections.content:
A bundle is created by setting createAndGo(4) in mfrBundleRowStatus. An agent may also support createAndWait(5) followed by a set to active(1). When a bundle is created, the agent must create a new interface in the ifTable, and that ifIndex becomes the value of mfrBundleIfIndex.

A bundle link is created by setting createAndGo(4) in mfrBundleLinkRowStatus. It is tied to a specific physical interface and uses that interface's ifIndex. Its row may be created after or during creation of the physical interface's row, and the bundle named in the row must already exist.
sections.eli5: To make a bundle you fill in a new form and say go. To add a wire to it, the bundle has to exist first.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
The linkUp and linkDown traps come from RFC 2223. For a bundle, linkUp is sent when its ifOperStatus goes from down to up, which happens when enough links are operationally up as determined by mfrBundleActivationClass and mfrBundleThreshold. linkDown is sent when it goes from up to down because too few links are up.

For a bundle link, linkUp is sent when mfrBundleLinkState becomes mfrBundleLinkStateUp, and linkDown when it leaves that value.

A third trap, mfrMibTrapBundleLinkMismatch, reports that a bundle link mismatch was detected, together with the configured and reported near-end and far-end names. The mfrBundleLinkMismatch counter is incremented when the trap is sent.
sections.eli5: The bundle rings a bell when it switches on or off, and each helper rings one too. A special bell rings if the two ends do not agree on who is talking to whom.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. These may be sensitive or vulnerable in some networks, and allowing SET operations without protection can harm network operation. The RFC states that no managed object in the MIB contains sensitive information.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, even on a secure network, because there is no control over who may GET or SET the objects. Implementers are advised to consider SNMPv3 security, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). The RFC makes it the customer's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate users can read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: Some of the dials can change how the network works, so only the right people should be allowed to turn them. Better locks exist in newer versions of SNMP.
